title: gpu-utilization-occupancy-nsight-analysis
content:
Summary:

This is a working analysis of recent Nsight runs for our serving runtime focusing on GPU utilization and occupancy for the transformer inference hotpaths (attention, fused-kernels, GEMM). The aim was to identify bottlenecks visible in kernel timelines, quantify achieved occupancy, and produce prioritized mitigation options to improve throughput and reduce latency variance.

Context & objectives:
- Target environment: single-GPU inference on NVIDIA A100-40GB (sm-8.0), CUDA 12.1, driver 525.105.17. Runtime: Redwood serving-runtime v0.7.2 with custom fused attention kernels and CUDA Graphs enabled for the main inference loop.
- Workload: 8k-token max sequence, typical inference batch sizes 1–8 (mostly 1 and 4). Model variant: LLaMA-like 22B, quantized to fp16 with custom attention fusion.
- Objectives:
  - Measure GPU-level utilization (%SM active, achieved occupancy) per kernel.
  - Identify kernels with low occupancy or memory-bound behavior.
  - Validate CUDA Graphs benefits and check for serialization points (synchronizations, unexpected memcpy).
  - Provide next-step experiments and quick wins.

What we ran:
- Nsight Systems trace (nsys) over 50 consecutive inferences for batch sizes 1, 4. Captured timeline of kernels, memcpy HtoD/DtoH, and stream concurrency. (artifact: nsight_run_2026-02-18.nsys-rep)
- Nsight Compute (ncu) focused runs on heavy kernels: attention_forward, fused_mha, ff_gemm, layer_norm, embedding_lookup. Collected achieved_occupancy, sm_efficiency, memory_throughput, l2_hit_rate (artifact: ncu_report_attention_kernel_2026-02-19.ncu-rep).
- Microbenchmarks: batched GEMM with cublasLt to compare kernel runtimes in isolation; measured tensor core utilization.

High-level observations from timeline:
- End-to-end forward pass median: ~118 ms (batch=1), ~320 ms (batch=4).
- Dominant kernels (batch=1): fused_mha (~42 ms, 35.6% of total), ff_gemm (~28 ms, 23.7%), embedding_lookup + gather (~9 ms), layer_norm+other (~7 ms). Small but frequent memcpy H2D for dynamic token index arrays (~6 ms total across trace).
- GPU occupancy and SM utilization trends vary by kernel: attention-related kernels show decent SM utilization but lower achieved occupancy (~32–40%) due to high per-thread register usage and resulting low active warps. Large GEMM kernels (cuBLAS) show high tensor-core utilization and good occupancy (~70–85%).

Nsight Compute detailed findings (selected):
- attention_forward kernel (custom fused):
  - achieved_occupancy: 34%
  - sm_efficiency: 58%
  - registers_per_thread: 128–160 (varies by sequence length code-path)
  - l2_throughput: moderate, L2 hit rate ~62%
  - memory bound? roofline indicates mixed compute-memory; arithmetic intensity low for some ops (indexed loads).
- fused_mha (alternative fused kernel):
  - achieved_occupancy: 29%
  - warp_execution_efficiency: 82%
  - stalls: high due to long-latency memory accesses and register dependencies
- ff_gemm (dense FFN GEMM using cuBLASLt):
  - achieved_occupancy: 78%
  - tensor_core_utilization: high (70–90%) when using fp16 paths
  - memory throughput near peak for the op window (bandwidth-limited at times)

Interpretation / root causes:
- Low achieved occupancy in custom attention kernels is driven largely by high register pressure and large per-thread local state (indexing, offsets, KV pointer math). The kernel launches are configured with block sizes that, combined with registers used, prevent many blocks from being resident per SM.
- Some attention code-paths do non-coalesced loads for variable-length token ranges (gather/scatter for attention masks and variable past KV lengths), increasing memory stall cycles and reducing SM efficiency.
- CUDA Graph capture reduces driver overhead and stream scheduling costs (see nsys timeline: reduced CPU->GPU gaps during batched capture), but we still see serialization around dynamic token index allocation (host-side) and small synchronous memcpy calls.
- cuBLAS-backed FFN is well-optimized (tensor cores) and not the bottleneck for occupancy; attention/fused kernels dominate latency.

Immediate actionable recommendations (quick wins):
1) Reduce register pressure in attention kernels:
   - Audit local arrays and temporaries; move rarely-used temporaries to shared memory when safe.
   - Recompile kernels with --maxrregcount tuned (experiment with values 64, 96, 112) and measure occupancy vs instruction count tradeoff.
2) Kernel launch parameters:
   - Increase blocks-per-grid by reducing threads-per-block when it doesn’t harm vectorization (e.g., move from 256 to 128 threads where possible) to allow more concurrent blocks per SM.
3) Memory access improvements:
   - Rework gather/indirect loads into coalesced patterns by rearranging KV storage layout or using precomputed, coalesced tile loads.
   - Introduce small per-block staging in shared memory for variable-length token index windows.
4) Move token index preparations into the CUDA Graph capture path and pre-allocate device buffers to remove small synchronous host->device memcpys seen in timeline.
5) Async memcpy + streams:
   - Switch small memcpy calls to async copies on a dedicated copy stream and ensure overlap with compute where safe.
6) Consider persistent threads / grid-stride loops for attention kernels that allow better SM occupancy for variable sequence lengths.
7) Continue using cuBLASLt for FFN and ensure FP16/Tensor core code-path selected consistently.

Planned experiments (priority order):
- Experiment A (low risk): compile attention kernels with maxrregcount=96 and profile occupancy + instruction throughput. Measure perf for sequences of length 128, 512, 2048.
- Experiment B (moderate): refactor KV layout to tile-major order, implement per-block shared loads for attention window, run nsys + ncu.
- Experiment C (higher effort): implement CUDA Graph capture end-to-end including device-side precomputed index buffers + remove host syncs. Measure latency tail and proportion of idle gaps in nsys timeline.
- Experiment D (exploratory): rework fused_mha to persistent-thread pattern; evaluate throughput at batch sizes 1 and 4.

Measurement plan and success criteria:
- For each experiment capture: nsight-systems trace (50 inferences) and ncu for 5 slowest kernels. Record median and p95 latency, achieved_occupancy, sm_efficiency, and memory throughput.
- Success targets:
  - Increase achieved_occupancy of attention kernels from ~34% -> >=50% without increasing single-kernel latency by >10% (i.e., avoid heavy register spilling).
  - Reduce end-to-end median latency by 15% (batch=1) and p95 by 20% after combined changes.
  - Reduce small host->device memcpy count to zero during steady-state inference.

Notes / gotchas observed in runs:
- NCU reports sometimes differ by 2–5% between successive runs due to L2 effects and thermal throttling—always run 3 repeats.
- Enabling aggressive register limits can push compiler to spill to local memory and erase gains; watch for increased local memory throughput in ncu.
- A100 has high SM count; occupancy improvements have diminishing returns if kernel is memory-bound—use roofline to validate.

Attachments and artifacts:
- Nsight Systems capture: drive://captures/nsight_run_2026-02-18.nsys-rep (timeline with stream names annotated)
- Nsight Compute reports: drive://captures/ncu_report_attention_kernel_2026-02-19.ncu-rep (attention), drive://captures/ncu_report_ff_gemm_2026-02-19.ncu-rep (ffn)
- Microbenchmark scripts and cublasLt test: GitHub PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/482

Next steps / owners (short):
- Asha: run Experiment A (compile variants with maxrregcount) and post updated ncu reports by 2026-02-26.
- Miguel: prototype shared-memory staging for KV tile loads (Experiment B) and push a draft PR for review by 2026-03-04.
- Sofia: add CUDA Graph capture for token index buffers in a sandbox branch and measure timeline improvements by 2026-03-02.
- Daniel: re-run end-to-end benchmarks with stable power profile (persistence mode) and collect 10-run averages for latency p95.

Open questions / discussion points to resolve:
- How aggressive can we be with decreasing register count before local-memory spill becomes net-negative? (need numeric tradeoff experiments)
- Is it acceptable to change KV layout at the runtime level (breaking cache compatibility) for better coalescing? Product/compatibility input required.
- Should we prioritize persistent-thread refactor (higher effort) or incremental register/layout improvements first?

If you want I can attach short extracts of the nsys timeline and the specific NCU counters we care about (achieved_occupancy, sm__warps_active.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_active_warps, lts__t_bytes.sum) into a follow-up document for the PR review.
